content:
I would like to work on a formalisation of Desargues's theorem which could eventually be integrated into mathlib. To my knowledge, even though there have been some attempts and discussions about this, there is still no full proof (at least a human one).

As a proof of concept, I do have a working formalisation of the general version here, but it is by no means good (at the time of writing, I was very new to Lean, and it is solely focused on proving the result). I want to do it in a way which would adhere to the library's standards. This is quite a large undertaking, so I'm curious about the community's opinions on how exactly we should approach it (and whether there is interest at all).

The natural setting for Desargues's theorem is projective geometry. Now, one could simply do it algebraically in homogeneous coordinates, but the synthetic approach is much more elegant and closer to how we think about geometry (and also in the mathlib spirit of maximal generality). Therefore, the plan is as follows:

  1. Start from Mathlib.Combinatorics.Configuration and define a projective geometry as a configuration (point set with lines) satisfying certain axioms.
  2. Prove that there is a natural matroidal structure on a projective geometry, which will give us access to well-behaved notions such as independence, basis, dimension and subspace. Further, this matroid has nice properties such as finitarity and modularity.
  3. Prove Desargues's theorem for projective geometries of dimension at least three (it does not hold for planes).
  4. Prove that the projectivisation of a module over a skew-field defines a projective geometry. From this, deduce the other versions of Desargues's theorem (for dimension 2, it holds because the projectivisation can be embedded into a projectivisation of dimension 3).

All in all, it seems like a result which is among the most easily achievable among the missing theorems of "the 100". What's more, after this, there is potential for more results of synthetic projective geometry, such as the Veblen-Young theorem (the projective geometries of dimension at least three are precisely the projectivisations of modules over skew-fields) and the role of Pappus's theorem (it holds exactly when the skew-field is commutative).
CC @Joseph Myers as our Euclidean geometry expert

I agree that it's good for mathlib to prove Desargues in a projective context and then deduce affine versions from that. (Having affine space versions will be useful for applying it on Euclidean geometry problems. But there will probably be quite a lot of such versions, because of all the different possibilities for which points are at infinity.)

Similarly proving projectively and then deducing affine / Euclidean versions would make sense for Pascal's theorem (another missing one of 100 theorems) (and likewise Brianchon).

Thanks! To be honest, I'm not sure how helpful this axiomatic setting would be for Pascal's theorem (Brianchon is just the dual, so that should be easy afterwards), the algebraic approach would probably be better (maybe as a simple consequence of the Cayley-Bacharach theorem; but I don't know how far mathlib is in that regard). However, there are interesting results in the axiomatic alley as well, such as that of Buekenhout stating that if Pascal's theorem holds for an oval (a synthetic concept generalising a conic), the projective plane is pappian (i.e., the projectivisation of a vector space; precisely the scenario in the algebraic approach) and the oval is a conic.

My comments are only about the high-level structure (prove projective results in a projective context before deducing affine / Euclidean results for more convenient application in that context) rather than about exactly how you go about proving the projective results.

As for the particular statement of the general Desargues's theorem, I think it would be more practical to use collinearity rather than speaking about lines defined by some points and their intersections (that would need many assumptions on which points are different and not collinear), even though it may look a little awkward. So what I imagine is like this (generalising Collinear and Triangle from affine spaces):

variable {P L : Type*} [Membership P L]
-- `P` are the points, `L` are the lines

def points (l : L) :  Set P := {p | p ∈ l}

variable (L)
def Collinear (S : Set P) : Prop := ∃ l : L, S ⊆ points l

structure Triangle where
  points : Fin 3 → P
  independent : ¬ Collinear L (.range points)
-- this is for illustration, once we have the matroidal structure,
-- simplices would be defined via independence
variable {L}

def InCentralPerspectiveFrom (c : P) (T₁ T₂ : Triangle L) : Prop :=
  Collinear L {T₁.points 0, T₂.points 0, c}
    ∧ Collinear L {T₁.points 1, T₂.points 1, c}
    ∧ Collinear L {T₁.points 2, T₂.points 2, c}

def InCentralPerspective (T₁ T₂ : Triangle L) : Prop := ∃ c, InCentralPerspectiveFrom c T₁ T₂

def InAxialPerspective (T₁ T₂ : Triangle L) : Prop :=
  ∃ r₀ r₁ r₂ : P, Collinear L {r₀, r₁, r₂}
    ∧ (Collinear L {r₀, T₁.points 1, T₁.points 2} ∧ Collinear L {r₀, T₂.points 1, T₂.points 2})
    ∧ (Collinear L {T₁.points 0, r₁, T₁.points 2} ∧ Collinear L {T₂.points 0, r₁, T₂.points 2})
    ∧ (Collinear L {T₁.points 0, T₁.points 1, r₂} ∧ Collinear L {T₂.points 0, T₂.points 1, r₂})

variable (P L)
def DesarguesProperty : Prop :=
  ∀ {T₁ T₂ : Triangle L}, InCentralPerspective T₁ T₂ ↔ InAxialPerspective T₁ T₂
-- in practice, this would be implemented as a typeclass extending projective geometries

Does that seem reasonable?

I don't have advice on the details of what the projective definitions and API should look like. Presumably you'll discover while setting things up for abstract projective spaces whether what you have works well or not.

There is also what is presumably an awful AI written formalization of Desargues at https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/HundredTheorems/Theorem87.lean#L510.

I'm not encouraging anyone to look at it, but if anyone (or their AI) ever forms an opinion of whether it is awful or not I would be interested to hear (mostly because this is a theorem on the Freek list, so this AI written proof will likely be linked to soon).
